Well, Dr. ____, I’m here because... well, it’s a long story, but for almost two years now, I’ve been dealing with this situation that I just cannot shake, and it's completely exhausting me. I’m a music director and a composer, and right after this major commission I had—which was supposed to be this huge, positive turning point for me after finishing my graduate degree—things just took a turn. 

I have this absolute certainty, and I mean I know it in my bones, that a few specific people in the ensemble started quietly working together to undermine my work. And they don't do it out in the open where I can just stop the baton and address it. It’s all these incredibly calculated, subtle things. They’ll use sudden schedule changes that just happen to rob us of the most critical rehearsal time for my pieces, or they'll make these very specific seating choices that completely ruin the acoustic balance I'm trying to build in the string section. And then there are these little comments... just these tiny, quiet remarks during rehearsals that are designed to throw off my focus or undermine my authority with the rest of the players. 

And the most frustrating part, the reason my head feels like it's spinning all the time, is that whenever I try to bring it up, they have these perfect excuses ready to go. They’ll actually pull up emails or forward me administrative notes that supposedly explain why the rehearsal room was double-booked, or why the seating chart had to be adjusted for spacing, as if that proves it was all just an innocent clerical error. But I know what I'm seeing. You don't just accidentally sabotage a director's work for almost two years straight. No matter how much supposed proof or documentation they show me, I know exactly what they are doing to me, and it's making it nearly impossible to do my job.

Voices? No, no, definitely not. I mean... well, as a composer, obviously my head is always full of sound, right? Like, if I'm working on a new orchestration, I can close my eyes and hear the brass section coming in, or I can hear the exact timbre of the cellos against the violas. I'm not sitting here hearing phantom people talking to me out of thin air or anything like that. My hearing is actually incredibly sharp, which is probably why I pick up on all their little whispered comments during rehearsal in the first place when they think I'm focused on the woodwinds. I hear exactly what is actually there, in the room. So no, no imaginary voices.

A special message? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, there’s no outside force or... or mystical power at play here. It’s actually incredibly mundane, which in a way makes it even more infuriating. It’s just pure, calculated, professional jealousy and resentment.

It’s entirely human, incredibly petty, and entirely grounded in the reality of orchestral politics.

They don't need an outside force to be vindictive, they just need an ego and a willingness to ruin a good piece of music just to put me in my place. So, no, no special powers or secret messages. Could I be wrong? No, I... I mean, I'm here, aren't I? I'm talking to you because for almost two years now, I've been completely unable to shake this certainty. No, no, nothing like that. Like I said earlier, my life outside of this job is perfectly normal. I mean, I go home, I work on my scores, I listen to recordings, I occasionally meet up with a few friends from grad school who aren't affiliated with this particular ensemble... and everything is fine. I'm a very rational, analytical person. You have to be, to do what I do. Composing and directing—it's essentially architecture with sound. It requires logic, structure, an understanding of form and proportion. I approach my whole life that way. I pay my rent on time, I go to the dentist, I buy my groceries at the same market every Sunday morning. There's absolutely nothing out of the ordinary about my day-to-day existence, except for the fact that when I step onto that podium, I am stepping into a completely manufactured, hostile environment. 

If I were the kind of person who just naturally had bizarre ideas or thought the whole world was out to get me, don't you think it would bleed into other areas of my life? I'd be having issues with my landlord, or fighting with the barista at the coffee shop, or convinced that my friends were secretly plotting against me. But none of that is happening. The only place I have any kind of conflict, the only place where I'm experiencing this... this targeted campaign, is with those specific musicians in that specific hall. So no, outside of the ensemble, my life is completely, entirely mundane. Boring, even, if you don't count the music.

It's the schedule changes that always happen at the worst possible moment. You don't just have that many consecutive accidents that all specifically target one person's ability to do their job. So no, I'm not wrong. I know exactly what they're doing, no matter how many emails they wave in my face to try and prove otherwise.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had times when your thoughts felt jumbled or hard to follow, or other people said you were making little sense?\n\nPatient: Jumbled? Like I said earlier, my life outside of this job is perfectly normal. It's completely fine. I don't walk down the street thinking people are following me, I don't think the government is tapping my phone, I don't believe in aliens or ghosts or... whatever else you might consider an \"unusual belief.\" \n\nI'm a very rational, analytical person. You have to be, to do what I do. Composing and directing—it's essentially architecture with sound. It requires logic, structure, an understanding of form and proportion. I approach my whole life that way. I pay my rent on time, I go to the dentist, I buy my groceries at the same market every Sunday morning. Odd? Eccentric? No, not at all. I mean, look at me, look at how I dress. I'm just wearing a standard button-down shirt and slacks. But no, nobody has ever called me odd. If anything, I've been told by my mentors that I'm almost too analytical, too structured for a creative field. I color inside the lines, socially speaking. I always have. 

So this idea that I might be some eccentric weirdo who just naturally rubs people the wrong way because I'm out of touch with reality or because I act strangely... that's just not me. Look, the thing about "clear proof" is... well, what even constitutes proof in a situation like this? Because they actually *have* tried to show me things. I mean, that's really the whole crux of it, that's why I'm here talking to you today. Because for almost two years now—ever since that big commission, which honestly should have been a massive high point in my career, something to celebrate—I’ve just been completely unable to shake this absolute certainty about what they're doing. 

It’s a few specific people in the ensemble, and they’ve been using all these incredibly subtle tactics to quietly undermine my work. And they are subtle, which is what makes it so maddening. I'm talking about sudden schedule changes that just happen to conflict with when I need the hall, or very deliberate seating choices that completely mess with the acoustics and the balance I'm trying to build for a piece, and then these... these little comments in rehearsals. Just under their breath, or phrased as innocent questions about the tempo or the bowing, but they aren't innocent. They're designed to make the rest of the players doubt my direction.

And the frustrating part, to your question about proof, is that they *do* produce these so-called explanations. When I call them out on it, they'll forward me emails or pull up notes from the administration or the stage manager that supposedly explain why the seating had to change or why the rehearsal time was bumped. They wave these printouts in my face like, "See? It's just an administrative error, the hall was double-booked, look at this memo!" 

So even when they show me these emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away as some big string of harmless accidents, it doesn't change anything for me. I can't just turn off what I know is happening. If someone I trusted, like my wife, looked at those same emails... I mean, she might think it looks like an accident on paper, sure, because these musicians are very careful about how they document things. They know how to cover their tracks. But paper doesn't capture the tone of those little comments in the hall, does it? An email doesn't capture the smirks when I have to stop the rehearsal to fix a seating arrangement they purposely messed up. 

So, no, even with their "proof," I wouldn't change my mind. I can't shake the certainty. It's been two years of this constant, quiet sabotage since the commission. You just don't have two solid years of perfectly timed "accidents" that only ever seem to negatively impact my time on the podium.

There's absolutely nothing out of the ordinary about my day-to-day existence, except for the fact that when I step onto that podium, I am stepping into a completely manufactured, hostile environment. \n\nIf I were the kind of person who just naturally had bizarre ideas or thought the whole world was out to get me, don't you think it would bleed into other areas of my life? I'd be having issues with my landlord, or fighting with the barista at the coffee shop, or convinced that my friends were secretly plotting against me. But none of that is happening. The only place I have any kind of conflict, the only place where I'm experiencing this... this targeted campaign, is with those specific musicians in that specific hall. So no, outside of the ensemble, my life is completely, entirely mundane. Boring, even, if you don't count the music.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe this sabotage is part of a larger, implausible plot with an impossible or bizarre explanation, or does it still seem like a realistic workplace scheme to you?\n\nPatient: Implausible? Bizarre? No, no, not at all. I mean, I'm not sitting here telling you they're using mind control or, I don't know, intercepting my thoughts through the baton or something ridiculous like that. It's completely realistic. It's almost painfully realistic, which is why it's so frustrating that nobody else seems to want to acknowledge it. It's just a classic, albeit highly coordinated, workplace scheme. \n\nYou see this kind of thing in the arts all the time, honestly. It's a very competitive field. Egos get bruised easily. I came in, I was young, I got this commission that a lot of older, more established people probably felt they deserved, or at least they felt I *didn't* deserve. And so they formed a little clique. It's just human nature, really, just taken to a very toxic extreme. They talk behind my back, they coordinate their little disruptions—the late scores, the chair shuffling, the whispered conversations right when I need the room's attention. It's all very mundane, logistical sabotage. \n\nThere's no grand, impossible conspiracy here. It's not the Illuminati. It's just three or four bitter musicians who have decided they don't like me, they don't respect my authority on the podium, and they want to make my job as difficult as humanly possible so that I either quit or I look so incompetent that the board decides not to renew my contract. That's it. It's just petty, vindictive, coordinated workplace bullying. And the fact that they use the bureaucracy of the ensemble—the venue manager, the librarian, the operations manager—to cover their tracks just proves how realistic and grounded the whole thing is. They know exactly how to manipulate the system to make it look like a string of accidents. It's infuriating, but it's certainly not bizarre.\n\nDoctor: Have you had similar suspicions that other people were trying to undermine or take advantage of you in other parts of your life, like with friends, family, or neighbors?\n\nPatient: No, no, not at all. Like I was saying before, this is strictly contained to the hall. It's just them. My life outside of that building is completely fine, honestly. I don't look at my neighbors and think they're stealing my mail, I don't think my friends from grad school are talking about me behind my back. I mean, my wife and I, things are basically steady at home. We have our normal routines. We cook dinner together, we watch a movie, we talk about her day... she's a graphic designer, so she has her own client issues, but it's nothing like what I'm dealing with. But between us? No suspicion, no tension, nothing like that. \n\nAnd my own work—my solitary work, I mean—is going perfectly well. Outside of this issue with the ensemble, I still meet all my deadlines for commissions. I'm keeping up with my composing. I sit at my piano in the mornings, and the ideas flow just fine. I'm not distracted by some overarching paranoia. I even still run most mornings. I get up at 6:00 AM, I run my usual four-mile loop around the park near our apartment, and I don't spend that time looking over my shoulder or wondering if the guy walking his golden retriever is secretly working for the principal cellist. \n\nI'm telling you, it's just this one specific group of people in this one specific context. If I were just a generally paranoid person who thought everyone was out to get me, I wouldn't be able to sit down and write a thirty-minute symphony movement, would I? I wouldn't be able to just go for a jog and enjoy the morning air. I'd be a wreck. But I'm not a wreck. I'm highly functional in every single other aspect of my life. It's only when I have to stand in front of those specific musicians, knowing what they're doing to undermine me, that there's any problem at all. My friends, my family, my wife... they're my support system. I trust them completely.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had the feeling that people in other settings, like strangers or coworkers elsewhere, were trying to harm, monitor, or undermine you too?\n\nPatient: I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, Doctor, but... no. Actually, I just turned in a completely separate string quartet piece two weeks ahead of schedule. I keep up with my composing every single day. I sit at the piano in my apartment, I work out the voicings, the counterpoint, and the music flows exactly the way it always has. Nobody is sneaking in to erase my hard drive or alter my sheet music. \n\nAnd things at home with my wife are basically steady, just like I was saying. We just go about our normal, everyday lives. She works on her graphic design layouts in the living room, I work on my orchestrations in the study, we make dinner—usually something simple, like pasta, because by the end of the day we're both pretty drained—and that's it. There's no one trying to harm me, there's no one monitoring my emails, there's no grand conspiracy in my neighborhood or at the grocery store. It is literally just that one hall, with those specific musicians, during those specific rehearsals. I don't know how else to explain that my life is incredibly, almost boringly normal everywhere else.\n\nDoctor: Have you always been seen as unusually odd or eccentric in the way you think, dress, or relate to people, even before this rehearsal conflict started?\n\nPatient: Odd? Eccentric? No, not at all. I mean, look at me, look at how I dress. I'm just wearing a standard button-down shirt and slacks. When I'm working, when I'm on the podium, it's the standard black suit, maybe a dark turtleneck if we're doing a contemporary piece, but nothing flashy. I don't wear capes or, I don't know, mismatched neon socks to make some sort of avant-garde statement. We just get along like normal people.\n\nIf anything, I'm actually known for being very organized and pragmatic, which you absolutely have to be if you're going to direct an ensemble. I always have. \n\nSo this idea that I might be some eccentric weirdo who just naturally rubs people the wrong way because I'm out of touch with reality or because I act strangely... that's just not me. Physical harm? Like... like actually attack me? Oh, no. No, no, no. I mean, I can see why you might ask that, given how intense and stressful this whole situation is, but no, I've never once worried about my physical safety.

Me? Suspicious of everyone? Oh, no. No, not at all. Honestly, before all of this started—before the commission, before the ensemble turned on me—I was probably one of the most trusting people you could meet. Maybe even too trusting, if I'm being perfectly honest with myself.

Wait, did... I mean, I feel like we literally just went over this with the whole David and Sarah thing, right? But, okay, to be absolutely, one-hundred-percent clear—no. Not at all. I never preferred being alone, and I have always, always had a huge interest in close relationships.
